title: Love that lets go
hook: sometimes love means letting someone go

segments.voice: Yesterday, the earth, and Francis calling it sister and mother. Your line was sister earth. Which patch of ground did you get to look after? Today, a harder kind of care: the kind that opens its hands. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

The car is packed to the roof. A lamp, a laundry basket, a box marked kitchen in thick marker. A parent stands in a dorm hallway that smells of fresh paint, and the hardest part of the day is not the stairs. It's the moment of walking back to the car alone. Every instinct says stay one more hour, fix one more shelf, check the lock on the window again. And the kid, very kindly, is already looking past them at the people down the hall. Nothing has gone wrong. This is what it looked like when everything went right. Today: love that lets go.
screen: `THE CAR PACKED TO THE ROOF.` → `WALKING BACK ALONE.` → `WHEN EVERYTHING WENT RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Start with a story Jesus tells in the Gospel of Luke, known as the prodigal son. The ending, the son coming home, gets the attention. Look at the beginning instead. The younger son asks for his share of the family money early, while his father is still alive. In the old King James Bible it reads: "Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth to me. And he divided unto them his living." That's it. No lecture is recorded. No conditions. The father lets him go. Second, the waiting. When the son finally turns back, the story says the father saw him while he was "yet a great way off." Some readers notice what that means: he had been watching the road. Letting go did not mean he stopped loving. It meant he loved without holding the door shut. Third, a voice from a very different shelf of the Bible. The book of Ecclesiastes sets life out as a list of seasons, and two of its lines land right here: "a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing," and "a time to keep, and a time to cast away." The book doesn't say which time you're in. It only says both are real. Fourth, Buddhist teaching has a word for the opposite of this kind of love: clinging. In the Buddha's first sermon, craving is named as the origin of suffering, and love that clings starts to squeeze. Letting go, for them, isn't coldness. It's love that has stopped needing to own. Set them side by side: the father, the seasons, the open hand. Releasing someone can be an act of love, not the end of it.
screen: `HE DIVIDED UNTO THEM HIS LIVING.` · `YET A GREAT WAY OFF.` · `A TIME TO REFRAIN FROM EMBRACING.` · `LOVE THAT STOPS CLINGING.` · then, large: `LOVE THAT LETS GO.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest wherever they fall, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one person you're holding tightly right now. A child growing up, a friend moving away, someone whose choices aren't yours to make, someone who has already gone. Now notice those hands. If they've curled, let them rest open on your knees. Hold that person in mind with your hands open. You don't have to stop caring. Just let the grip ease, a little, for a few breaths. If you pray, you can place them in God's keeping in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Prodigal son. The parable where a father lets his son go, then watches the road, loving without holding the door shut. Today's word.

Your line: let go, lovingly. Once today, when you feel yourself reaching to control what someone you love is doing, open your hand instead and tell them you're in their corner. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: People on many paths practice letting go in their own ways: Christians may entrust someone to God in prayer, Buddhist teachers speak of loosening clinging in meditation, and families mark leavings with blessings, meals or small rituals.

fork.setup: you're the father. your younger son asks for his share of everything, now, while you're still alive. what do you do?
options: refuse, and tell him he isn't ready.
divide the living and let him go.
give it, but follow him to keep watch.
fork.reveal: he divides his living, and the son leaves. no lecture is recorded. later the father sees him "yet a great way off". some readers take it that he had kept watching the road.

original.note: Hebrew: a time, a season, the word Ecclesiastes uses in its list of seasons.

trapdoor: what you thought: letting go means you've stopped loving.
what it means: releasing someone into their own life, while still caring.
what a scholar hears: Luke's father divides his living without a recorded word, and Ecclesiastes sets embracing and refraining side by side as seasons.
recall: love is a decision and a promise
goodwill for all, asking nothing back
